steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on using an artificial neural network to predict the key length of the Vigenère cipher. Set it in the context of ANNs in historical cryptology, explain why the key length matters, review the existing key-length methods briefly, say what our model does, and give the paper's outline.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have had a lot of applications throughout academia recently. Open-source software libraries like TensorFlow and Keras have been developed, and these make it possible to train and test ANNs quickly for many different purposes. In particular there have been a steady stream of applications to cryptanalysis questions in historical cryptology in the last 10 years, for example there are ANNs that have been created for cipher detection among sets of classical ciphers. In this paper we build an ANN for another important cryptanalysis question in historical cryptology, which is how we can accurately predict the key length of a Vigenère cipher.

The Vigenère cipher is one of the most well-studied historical ciphers. Its development can be traced back to the mid 1400s and several cryptologists were involved in it. A detailed description of the history of the Vigenère cipher can be found in Chapter 4 of another source. In this cipher a keyword of length k is used to give a sequence of k shifts, and these shifts are used repeatedly in order to encrypt. If a cryptanalyst knows that the key length is k, they can partition the ciphertext into k cosets, and each coset contains letters that were encrypted with the same shift (or the same alphabet if it is an arbitrary polyalphabetic substitution cipher). If these cosets are large enough, it is straightforward to finish breaking the cipher using frequency analysis, and there are examples that implement this technique. So it is important to have accurate and efficient algorithms for finding the key length first.

Existing algorithms (reviewed in detail in Section 2)
- Babbage–Kasiski test and index of coincidence: two most well known, applied for over a hundred years
- recently: twist-based algorithms
  - original twist algorithm: Barr–Simoson
  - improved twist + algorithm: Park–Kim–Cho–Yum
  - twist ++ algorithm: Millichap–Yau–Pate–Carns
- each has own strengths and weaknesses across key lengths / text lengths -> natural to build ANN using them, highlight strengths, mitigate weaknesses

Our ANN
- accurate prediction for large range of key lengths and text lengths
- uses classical tools (index of coincidence in variety of formats) + recent twist-based algorithms + a few other features (Section 3.3)
- Table 2: accuracy vs index of coincidence and twist-based algorithms; ANN clearly better for variety of text lengths

Organization
- Section 2: review of methods, strengths/weaknesses, all tested as potential features
- Section 3: creation, training, evaluation of the ANN

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have had a lot of applications throughout academia recently. Open-source software libraries like TensorFlow and Keras have been developed, and these make it possible to train and test ANNs quickly for many different purposes. In particular there have been a steady stream of applications to cryptanalysis questions in historical cryptology in the last 10 years, for example there are ANNs that have been created for cipher detection among sets of classical ciphers. In this paper we build an ANN for another important cryptanalysis question in historical cryptology, which is how we can accurately predict the key length of a Vigenère cipher.

The Vigenère cipher is one of the most well-studied historical ciphers. Its development can be traced back to the mid 1400s and several cryptologists were involved in it. A detailed description of the history of the Vigenère cipher can be found in Chapter 4 of another source. In this cipher a keyword of length k is used to give a sequence of k shifts, and these shifts are used repeatedly in order to encrypt. If a cryptanalyst knows that the key length is k, they can partition the ciphertext into k cosets, and each coset contains letters that were encrypted with the same shift (or the same alphabet if it is an arbitrary polyalphabetic substitution cipher). If these cosets are large enough, it is straightforward to finish breaking the cipher using frequency analysis, and there are examples that implement this technique. So it is important to have accurate and efficient algorithms for finding the key length first.

Several algorithms have been developed to predict the key length, and we review them in detail in Section 2. Historically the two most well known techniques are the Babbage–Kasiski test and the index of coincidence, and these have been applied for over a hundred years. More recently a series of papers introduced the twist-based algorithms, which are new approaches to predicting the key length. Barr–Simoson introduced the original twist algorithm. Park–Kim–Cho–Yum gave an improved version which is called the twist + algorithm. Millichap–Yau–Pate–Carns made further modifications to build the twist ++ algorithm. Each of these algorithms has its own strengths and weaknesses for a wide variety of key lengths and text lengths. So it is natural to build an ANN for key length prediction that uses these algorithms, in the hope of highlighting their individual strengths and mitigating their weaknesses.

In this paper we give an accurate model for predicting the key length of a Vigenère cipher for a large range of key lengths and text lengths. The ANN uses both classical tools (the index of coincidence in a variety of formats) and much more recent algorithms (the twist-based algorithms), and also a few other features. The exact features of our model are given in Section 3.3. We compare the accuracy with the index of coincidence and the twist-based algorithms in Table 2, and this clearly shows the superior accuracy of our ANN for a variety of text lengths.

The paper is organized like this. Section 2 reviews a variety of well-established methods from the literature for predicting the key length of a Vigenère cipher and analyzes their strengths and weaknesses. We tested all of these tools as potential features for our ANN. Section 3 discusses how we created, trained, and evaluated an ANN for finding the key length of the Vigenère cipher.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have recently seen many applications throughout academia. The development of open-source software libraries, such as TensorFlow and Keras, has made it possible to quickly train and test ANNs for a variety of purposes. In particular, there has been a steady stream of applications to cryptanalysis questions in historical cryptology in the last 10 years; see [1] and [2] for examples of ANNs created for cipher detection among sets of classical ciphers. Here, we build an ANN to attack another important cryptanalysis question in historical cryptology: how can we accurately predict the key length of a Vigenère cipher?

The Vigenère cipher is one of the most well-studied historical ciphers. Its development can be traced back to the mid 1400s and involved several cryptologists. We refer the reader to Chapter 4 of [3] for a detailed description of the history of the Vigenère cipher. For this cipher, a keyword of length k is used to designate a sequence of k shifts that are used repeatedly in order for encryption. Once a cryptanalyst knows the key length is k, they can partition the ciphertext into k cosets, each of which contains letters encrypted with the same shift (or the same alphabet for an arbitrary polyalphabetic substitution cipher). Assuming these cosets are large enough, it is a straightforward task to finish breaking the cipher via frequency analysis; see [4] for an example that implements this technique. This motivates the importance of having accurate and efficient algorithms for first finding the key length.

Several algorithms have been developed to predict the key length, which we review in detail in Section 2. Historically, the Babbage–Kasiski test [5] and the index of coincidence [6] are the two best known techniques, and they have been applied for over a hundred years. More recently, a series of papers have introduced twist-based algorithms as new approaches to predicting key length. The original twist algorithm was introduced by Barr–Simoson in [7]. Park–Kim–Cho–Yum provided an improved version, called the twist + algorithm, in [8]. Millichap–Yau–Pate–Carns made further modifications in [9] to build the twist ++ algorithm. For a wide variety of key lengths and text lengths, each of these algorithms has its own strengths and weaknesses. It is therefore natural to build an ANN for key length prediction that uses these algorithms, in the hope of highlighting their individual strengths while mitigating their weaknesses.

Our work provides an accurate model for predicting the key length of a Vigenère cipher for a large range of key lengths and text lengths. The ANN implements both classical tools (the index of coincidence in a variety of formats) and much more recent algorithms (twist-based algorithms), along with a few other features. Our exact model features are described in Section 3.3. Accuracy comparisons with the index of coincidence and the twist-based algorithms are given in Table 2, which clearly show the superior accuracy of our ANN for a variety of text lengths.

Our paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review a variety of well-established methods from the literature for predicting the key length of a Vigenère cipher and analyze their strengths and weaknesses. All of these tools were tested as potential features for our ANN. In Section 3, we discuss the creation, training, and evaluation of an ANN for finding the key length of the Vigenère cipher.

References:
[1] Kopal N., Of ciphers and neurons detecting the type of ciphers using artificial neural networks , Proceedings of the 3rd International Conference on HIstorical Cryptology, HistoCrypt 2020 (2020), no. 171, 77–86.
[2] Esslinger B. Lampesberger H. Hermann E. Leierzopf E., Kopal N., A massive machine-learning approach for classical cipher type detection using feature engineering , Proceedings of the 4th International Conference on Historical Cryptology, HistoCrypt 2021 (2021), no. 183, 111–120.
[3] D. Kahn, The codebreakers: The comprehensive history of secret communication from ancient times to the internet. , Scribner, New York, NY, 1996.
[4] Craig P. Bauer, Secret history—the story of cryptology , second ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC Cryptography and Network Security, CRC Press, Boca Raton, FL, 2021.

[6] Friedman W.F., ”the index of coincidence and its application in cryptography,” , Riverbank Laboratories Deparmtent of Ciphers Publication 22 (1920).
[7] Thomas H. Barr and Andrew J. Simoson, Twisting the keyword length from a vigenère cipher , Cryptologia 39 (2015), no. 4, 335–341, https://doi.org/10.1080/01611194.2014.988365 .
[8] Seongmin Park, Juneyeun Kim, Kookrae Cho, and Dae Hyun Yum, Finding the key length of a vigenère cipher: How to improve the twist algorithm , Cryptologia 44 (2020), no. 3, 197–204, https://doi.org/10.1080/01611194.2019.1657202 .
